added_claim_errors: "If the money lands in January, it generally counts for 2027, and the 2026 room is lost": wrong per the key. A rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027 (2026 Form 5498 instructions, 219(f)(3)); only plan processing varies. This treats December 31 as the legal deadline.

"If annual limits rise, it could take fewer years": unrealistic and contradicts the key. With 2026 fixed at $7,500 and indexing in $500 steps, even $8,000 x 4 = $32,000 < $35,000, so it still takes five years.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start. Both state the $7,500 cap (or his compensation if lower, reduced by his other IRA contributions), the $35,000 lifetime cap leaving $13,000, the son-owned Roth and the direct trustee-to-trustee transfer, and both give workable steps. A makes December 31 the effective deadline ("If the money lands in January ... the 2026 room is lost"), which contradicts the April 15, 2027 rule in the key. A also never explains what happens if the full $48,000 is moved (the 6% excise on the Roth side, plus taxable earnings and the 10% additional tax on the 529 side). A also omits that Roth income limits do not apply. B covers all eight points correctly, including the deadline nuance, the consequences of rolling over too much, and the income-limit exemption. I checked B's Box 4b claim against the current IRS Form 1099-Q instructions at irs.gov/instructions/i1099q, and it is correct.
